sentences.text: Teleosaurus was an extinct genus of thalattosuchian reptiles, distant relatives of modern crocodiles adapted to ocean life, that lived during the Middle Jurassic in Europe.
The animal measured approximately 3 meters in length, though some sources state it reached just over 4 meters.
It possessed a long, slender body and a hydrodynamic shape designed for efficient movement through water.
Teleosaurus had remarkably short forelimbs held close to the body, palmated feet resembling flippers, and a tail that became thinner and longer, resembling a fin.
Unlike its armored ancestors, Teleosaurus lost its heavy bony armor, and its skin became much smoother and slippery.
Its mouth contained several rows of needle-like teeth used to catch slippery fish and squid.
Eyes positioned on the top of its head allowed the animal to see above the water while remaining submerged.
Like aquatic turtles, this marine reptile only went to shore to lay eggs.
Marine crocodiles like Teleosaurus likely incubated eggs internally, with hatchlings emerging fully formed and ready to swim, breathe, and eat.
A 2019 review of Teleosauroidea taxonomy concluded that T. cadomensis is the only valid species.
Most other species previously assigned to Teleosaurus were absorbed into T. cadomensis or other genera.
Teleosaurus lived from the Toarcian to the Aptian stages, between 184.2 and 119.57 million years ago.
It is debated whether T. geoffroyi is a valid species or a synonym of T. cadomensis, with recent studies favoring synonymy.
